items.question: How do you assess the likelihood that AI will play a significant role in solving the next Millennium Prize problems?
items.object: AI's role in solving Millennium Prize problems

items.question: Why do you see mathematics as the right starting point for building an AI system?
items.object: Mathematics as the starting point for building an AI system
items.answer:
When we started the company, we had a really big focus on math. If you look around at all fields of science and engineering, well, almost all fields, math is really at their foundation, and math has essentially become the way that people understand the universe. It's the way you model phenomena from black holes to atoms. It's the way you design things in engineering.

There's a couple reasons for that. First of all, it just happens to be the case that the universe is explainable by math, so you can write down a fairly compact set of symbols that explain things. The other really important thing is that it's a way to build these shared cognitive theories that are very objective and clear and transparent. If you and I are discussing something that's rigorous, we can write down a set of deductive rules. We can agree on what the ground rules are of whatever we're modeling, and then from there we can derive conclusions.

With humans, what you see is that when people become very good at math, they tend to be good at other quantitative areas in science and engineering. Our bet is that if you make a system that's really good at math, you're probably going to see the same phenomenon, where it's true it might not immediately write the world's best history essays, but when you ask it to do something scientific or something in engineering, it's just going to be really, really good at that. That's why we started with math.

items.question: Why do you expect mathematical training to improve an AI model's ability to solve problems outside mathematics?
items.object: Transfer of mathematical training to problem solving outside mathematics
items.answer:
I'll give you the non-AI perspective. I studied math, and I was really good at math from when I was a little kid. I remember there were always the seventh graders in math class that would raise their hands whenever the teacher would come up with something, and it was always an abstract thing, like the side-angle-side of triangles. There'd be the annoying kid that was like, “When are we ever going to use this?” The teacher would kind of mumble a little bit, and they'd be like, “Well, math, you're probably not going to use it soon, but it'll make you really good at other things.” The other kids were always skeptical of that, and I bought into it. I just kept taking more and more advanced math. I went to Stanford and majored in it, then I went to grad school to do a math PhD.

My belief was that if I just focus on math, then I'm going to get really good at problem solving, and business problems and other problems will be easy compared to solving these really tough abstract algebra problem sets that I was banging my head against the wall for 10 hours every week trying to do. I think it basically ended up being correct. I didn't really pay attention to anything else. I took maybe one computer science class, intro to computer programming at Stanford, and five years later, when I became an entrepreneur, I found it really easy to pick up code. I found it really easy to pick up contracts. Of course, I'm no lawyer, but you could understand that stuff. The logical underpinnings are relatively simple compared to abstract algebra and analysis.

I think for humans at least, I consider myself an example of math transferring to other very monetizable things. For AI, my intuition seems to suggest that it should be the same. You already see a little bit of evidence of this. At this point it's an open secret in the industry that training on a lot of code data leads to much better performance on reasoning benchmarks. You can imagine what that'll look like when you have incredible math data sets that encompass a lot more general types of reasoning.

items.question: What do you find most remarkable about Terry Tao as a mathematician?
items.object: Terry Tao’s breadth as a mathematician
items.answer: I think what's really amazing about him is the breadth of the work. Most mathematicians get very deep into a pretty narrow domain, and Terry can get very deep across dozens of domains. He's made contributions to number theory, combinatorics, harmonic analysis, applied math. He's one of the leading Lean contributors at this point. I'm sure he's formalizing his papers in Lean and actually hopping on the community Zulip and engaging with students. He has a very popular blog, and I think the way that he's been able to do this is he's just smarter than 99.999% of people, probably even more than that. From a very early age, it was very clear that he was on another plane.

items.question: How do you see the mathematics community’s reception of AI and verification tools like Lean?

items.answer: I think it's split. It seems to be split. There's sort of the younger mathematicians, I think, are very pro-AI and pro-verification and tools like Lean, and I think the older folks are a little bit more skeptical. Not surprising. I think you see that in pretty much every field.

items.question: How do you think the role of human mathematicians will evolve as AI becomes better at mathematics?
items.object: The evolving role of human mathematicians as AI improves
items.answer:
My guess would be that this will evolve. My mental model is something like chess, where at first there will perhaps be a lengthy period of humans plus AI assist, and that will lead to a lot of really good results. Over time, I think the AI will get better and better. You look at chess right now, and it's sort of like if there's a human assisting the AI, the AI would be annoyed of it. They would just want to delete all of the input because it would only make the results worse. I'm not sure if we're going to get to that point. I think humans will at some point need to guide the algorithms, but I think the definition of what a mathematician will do will fundamentally change.

I was talking to one of my friends who's a mathematician at MIT, a young professor, very excited about the field. I asked him, when we were first starting this, “What do you think? Are you worried that you're in a field that is going to fundamentally change?” He's like, “The field of math has always changed. Back in the 1800s, mathematicians used to be in the Royal Court and they would be glorified calculators. They would solve quadratic equations by hand. Of course they were worried that when computers and calculators came out, the job would no longer exist. But mathematicians get to define what math is. I'm sure at some point it'll be prompting and guiding these AIs to solve problems.”

I think that's going to be very huge. Even if an AI solves the Riemann hypothesis, a human will always be in the loop because the humans posed the Riemann hypothesis to begin with. Just to add on that, in the future you're going to have a lot of compute resources dedicated to math, and the question will be a very human one: by which procedure do humans decide where to direct all that reasoning firepower? I think that's going to be the job of mathematicians. They have to choose what do we work on, how do we interpret the results, how do we interpret failures to find answers, that kind of thing.

items.question: Why do you think an AI math system should be capable of solving the Riemann hypothesis?
items.object: AI math systems’ ability to solve the Riemann hypothesis
items.answer: I think that it should be able to solve it, or prove that it's undecidable. That would also be an interesting result. If you think about what a great mathematician like Terry Tao is capable of doing, they're able to synthesize lots of papers, lots of frontier results, and learn from them in a way that the other top human mathematicians can, and find connections between these things and use them to create new and more complex theories. That's exactly how the system we're engineering works, and that's what computers are great at. AI models are great at synthesizing large amounts of information, finding patterns, recursively self-improving.

items.question: What excites you about mathematics as a domain for recursive AI self-improvement?
items.object: Mathematics as a domain for recursive AI self-improvement
items.answer: I think what a lot of people don't realize is that in these, let's say, perfectly observed zero-sum games, you improve recursively just by playing against yourself, but you hit an optimal strategy. At that point, it doesn't matter what system you have; it won't do better. The most exciting part about math is that there is no upper bound. You're just going to keep putting compute in, and it's going to keep getting better, and there's no end to it. When we talk about, do we think AI can solve a Riemann hypothesis or get a Millennium Prize, those are very human milestones. I think the real question is, will it ever stop? It clearly will get there, and I think we're going to end up solving problems that are much, much harder than the Riemann hypothesis, which we haven't even conceived of yet because it's almost beyond us to write down such a hard problem.

items.question: How do you understand Lean's value as a programming language for mathematics?
items.object: Lean as a programming language for mathematics
items.answer: Lean is just another programming language, a really great one created by Leonardo de Moura, the best programming language. We might all be writing Lean, or the AI might just be writing Lean in the future. The idea is that the mathematical statements are encoded in the type system of the language. Very simply, you have functions in Lean, and the input types correspond to the assumptions of the mathematical theorem, and the output type is the conclusion. The point of Lean is that if you write a program that implements that function and it compiles, that means you can derive the output type from the input type, which in turn implies that you can conclude the conclusion from the assumptions. That's the fundament. That's how you use Lean for math.

items.question: What do you find interesting about Lean's path from a software verification tool to widespread use in mathematics?
items.object: Lean's origins in software verification and adoption by mathematicians
items.answer:
One thing that's super interesting about Lean is if you look at Leonardo de Moura, the creator, who's at Amazon AWS now, he's not a mathematician, and he wrote this as a software verification tool. He has the belief that in the future software will be verified, and the existing tools, things like N and Isabelle, which are kind of multi-decade-old software verification tools, are just not good. They're frankly unusable; the experience for a developer is poor. He wanted to create a better software verification tool, in the hopes that if you build something better, more people will use it and we'll have better software, which is a super noble goal in its own right.

What he didn't realize was software verification, all it is is just proving that software has certain properties. This thing became very popular in the math community, and you had thousands of mathematicians and math students building up an organic library called Mathlib, which you can think of as the largest math textbook open source. It's on GitHub, and it's growing at a pretty fast clip. The usage of Lean for math, I think, to some degree has surpassed anyone's expectations. It might be more than the usage for verified software at this point. That might change as time goes forward.

items.question: Why do you think now is the right time for Harmonic to tackle AI theorem proving?
items.object: The timing of AI theorem proving and Harmonic’s founding
items.answer:
There are two really good reasons why now that we're excited about. First, the AI systems have gotten better in an interesting way. I was actually talking with a close friend about RL for theorem proving back in 2015 and 2016. One issue back then was that there wasn't even a great notion of an AI system that could predict something in an infinite action space. In Go, you can place a piece somewhere; it's either a black or white piece. But in math you can really do anything, like generate any next step. We didn't have great systems to do that. Autoregressive language models have gotten pretty good, so that's one thing that makes it possible. I'm talking on the time scale of a decade here, but that's really important.

The other thing that's kind of crazy is that Lean has gotten really good. If you had told a mathematician 20 years ago that a large fraction of the field would be excited about formal methods in math, they might have thought you were crazy. Back then formal methods were really isolated to formal logic or certain types of, maybe, graph theory. If you guys have heard of the Four Color Theorem, that was one big success for formal math. What's changed is that Lean is so flexible and so exciting for people that they've contributed this thing called Mathlib. Now there's a lot of body of knowledge that you can build on to prove things. The combination of AI starting to even be a possible fit for this problem, plus Lean working really well—and Lean 4 was only released officially in September 2023—really made it the right time to attack this.

items.question: Why do you see synthetic data as essential to training Harmonic's mathematical AI model?
items.object: Synthetic data for training Harmonic's mathematical AI model
items.answer: Synthetic data is the fuel for the model. There's an amazing resource called Mathlib, that open source repository. That's a lot of human-written Lean, and it's written in a way that's very general and compact, so they're really proving advanced theorems. It's not necessarily the best fit for problem solving, and as a result almost the only data you can use for this is synthetic data you generate yourself. That original data is not very applicable, so it's a data-poor regime compared to most areas of AI. The process that I described, where the agents themselves are trying to solve problems and thereby generate training signals, is the primary way in which you can get data. The other issue is that you have to progress through levels of intelligence. You're not necessarily proving the Riemann hypothesis up front; you're proving really simple things, but then you amplify yourself recursively throughout the process. Turns out there's not as much math data on the internet as cat videos.

items.question: Why do you think training on internet data creates a ceiling on AI capabilities?
items.object: Internet training data and self-play as paths to superhuman AI
items.answer: You can think of the actual internet data quality that's out there as providing a ceiling to how smart these models can get, because if you train on the cat videos and all the nice Wikipedia content and the internet content, it's an open problem how to get something that's significantly smarter than that. In our opinion, you do need to get into some kind of self-reinforcing self-play regime to get to a point where you can surpass the ability of human mathematicians and researchers at multiple tasks. In many ways, the path inevitably takes the AlphaGo to AlphaZero approach, and we learn how to make these models create the vast majority of their data and have the data actually increase in complexity as these models continue to iterate.

items.question: Why do you see mathematics as particularly well suited to training AI on increasingly complex problems?
items.object: Mathematics as a domain for recursive AI improvement
items.answer:
The great thing about math is there's a simple path to doing this. You can basically measure the complexity of a math problem and how difficult it is by how many lines of Lean it takes to solve. You can look at the complexity of a system, and a lot of problems are solved by breaking it down into smaller chunks and actually solving those chunks. The smaller chunks are more manageable because there are fewer lines to solve than the big one. If you get really good at that, and then get good at solving the chunks, then you can train your model to do better. As you keep turning the gears on that, the model gets better at solving incrementally harder and harder and more complex problems. I think that works very well in math because it mirrors how we solve math on pen and paper.

We've been able to start with simple axioms and build up giant complex structures. Maybe the Riemann hypothesis would be hundreds of pages, if not more, to solve. The Four Color Theorem was, I think, 200 pages, very, very complex. I do think eventually you'll get to a level where you'll be able to solve these things, and math is to some extent the original synthetic data.

items.question: How do you think energy and compute determine how fast your model can improve?
items.object: Energy and compute as drivers of model improvement
items.answer: The highest-level one is energy. The more energy you can put into it, the more attempts can happen in parallel, which means you generate data faster. There's a bunch of rate-limiting steps, but I don't see a fundamental constraint on how far, how fast it gets better. It's really just about how much compute you put in.

items.question: How do you see models overcoming the limitations of what's already formalized in Mathlib?
items.object: Mathlib's limitations and reliable autoformalization
items.answer: There's still a lot of unsolved problems in this field. We benefit a lot from core theorems that have been proved in the past. If you think about competition math context, there are theorems that every student would just learn and use, like AM-GM inequality, things of that nature. Mathlib is incomplete. There's very little content about geometry, for instance, and it's very theoretical and abstract. A limiting step is what's in Mathlib. Of course, at some point the models have to solve the problem of creating new theories and new structures, expanding to other domains and getting really, really good at formalizing things that haven't been formalized by humans. I think that'll be a big unlock, and that'll certainly happen within the next several years. You'll be able to say, “Here's just this situation,” it could be as simple as a baseball team and they're throwing balls back and forth to each other, and systems would be able to autoformalize that and turn that into Lean code on the fly. I don't think we're quite there yet, to the point where that's reliable, but when it does get reliable, I think that'll be a really big unlock.

items.question: What would success for Harmonic look like to you?
items.object: Harmonic's mission and ideal impact on mathematics
items.answer: Our mission statement is to explore the frontiers of human knowledge. It's very important to us that the things we produce are correct and useful to humans. In the best case, we're able to build a tool that a lot of mathematicians use to close all the Millennium Prize problems and go far beyond that. I think that'll be a great service to humanity.

items.question: How do you see systems that reason mathematically and check their reasoning changing software engineering?
items.object: Mathematical reasoning systems for software verification
items.answer: There's also other areas of commercial application for the software. The dream for software engineering is to be able to just check that code is correct. To do that, you need to have a very good model of how code works. You need to be able to understand how the libraries work, what they promise, that kind of thing. You can imagine a future where safety-critical software is proven correct, general software is proven correct, and the way software engineering is done can change as well. There are a lot of applications if you can make a system that's very good at math reasoning and very good at checking its reasoning.

items.question: Why would you personally value contributing to fundamental physics research?
items.object: Contributing to fundamental physics research
items.answer: I also think on the more theoretical side it's not just math, but physics is essentially math. Theoretical physics is one of the main ways the frontier of math gets implemented. I think it would be amazing to me personally to accelerate some of the fundamental physics research at the frontier and really just develop an understanding for why the universe is the way it is, why the laws of physics exist, and also help figure out experiments to test those. I would be very proud if we contributed to that effort.

items.question: What do you find most admirable about John von Neumann?
items.object: John von Neumann
items.answer: I like von Neumann. We were just talking before about von Neumann's biography. What I find really interesting about him was he started as a mathematician and he was discouraged. I think his father, who was a Hungarian businessman, was trying to discourage him from doing math because it wasn't very monetizable, and so he got his friend, who was a great mathematician, to try to talk him out of it. But the friend came back and he's like, “I can't do it. This guy's too good. It would be just a disservice to society if he didn't use his talents for math.” Then he pioneered computer science, and the von Neumann machine was the blueprint for all modern computers. He contributed to the Manhattan Project, which is a little controversial but very, very practical and impactful, and created probably the canonical text in game theory as well. I think he's pretty amazing. Also a fellow Eastern European, although some people debate whether Hungary is in Eastern Europe.

items.question: What do you find remarkable about Leibniz's idea of the universal characteristic?
items.object: Leibniz's universal characteristic
items.answer:
One thing people don't know is that Leibniz also had a lot of other work, and one piece of work that is incredibly prescient—keep in mind, this is the late 1600s—he created this idea called the universal characteristic, which is essentially the notion of having a deductive language, an automated procedure to deduce things using that language, and a body, an encyclopedia of work in that language that you can build on to derive things.

The amazing thing to me is that this thinker hundreds of years ago essentially predicted what would be happening in 2024, and it seems that the only thing that was required was having AI get a little better and having computers that can do something like Lean. I think it's incredible to have a human being predict that with no concept whatsoever of what's going to come later, but to understand that that's such a fundamental thing that we're going to end up working on.
